---
title: "Coherence constraints on pairwise decisions"
subtitle: "2.6 · after Kline, Rose and Walters (2024), Example 1"
description: "Compatibility of isolated-pair decisions with an ordered grade report."
---

Choosing the lowest-loss action for each pair separately need not yield a valid grade report. Moving middle firm B's posterior mean shows when coherence adds risk.


## Numerical illustrations {#what-to-try}

- **Middle at 1.00.** Isolated pairs withhold A–B and B–C while stating A above C (probability .921). Shared grades are transitive, so the best coherent reports reach risk .173.
- **Middle at .50.** B sits closer to C, so the pairwise choices print directly as {A} > {B, C} at risk .141.
- **Middle at .80.** Just below the shaded band, the pairwise choices still print as one report at risk .159.
- **Middle at 1.00, τ .10.** Lowering the withholding cost shifts the best coherent report to {A, B, C} at risk .100, withholding the confident outer pair too.
- **Middle at 1.00, τ .25.** The threshold drops to .75, below .760, so every pair is stated as {A} > {B} > {C} and the incoherent band disappears.

<details>
<summary>Transitivity and scope notes</summary>

Sharing a grade is transitive. If A shares a grade with B and B with C, the report must also withhold the comparison of A and C. Kline, Rose and Walters describe the conflict with the separate pair decisions as a “Condorcet cycle in indifferences.” These are posteriors set by hand for teaching. The browser evaluates every report of the stated family, lists equal-risk optima, and records their equal-risk tolerance in the disclosures.

</details>
